title: Lower abdominal pain in a 32-year-old teacher
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 32-year-old man in general practice with 12 hours of constant, dull periumbilical pain, nausea, vomiting, anorexia and fever, with pain on coughing and movement. The candidate then interprets a repeat set of observations and a urine dipstick, recognises probable acute appendicitis, arranges urgent hospital referral and answers his questions about the cause and complications.
focus: Recognising early acute appendicitis in general practice and arranging urgent surgical referral
stem: You are a medical student on placement at a general practice. Daniel Lando, a 32-year-old man, has come to the clinic because of abdominal pain. Your supervising GP has asked you to see him first. A practice nurse is available.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Lando and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Mr Lando's repeat observations and urine dipstick result. Hand him over to the surgical registrar, give your diagnosis and differentials, outline your management and answer his questions (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Daniel Lando, a 32-year-old full-time teacher. You are lying still on the examination couch and look uncomfortable. Moving and coughing make the pain worse, so you move carefully. You are worried but cooperative. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I've got this pain in my lower abdomen..." (point vaguely to the area around your belly button)

The pain (give only when asked):

  • Site: lower tummy, worst around the belly button. It doesn't go anywhere else.
  • Started about 12 hours ago, last night. It came on gradually.
  • It has been there constantly since then and hasn't changed. You've never had anything like it before.
  • Character: dull and hard to describe ("vague").
  • Severity: 7 out of 10. You've hardly done anything since it started.
  • Worse when you cough or move. Nothing makes it better.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • You feel feverish. You haven't taken your temperature.
  • You feel sick and vomited up your breakfast this morning.
  • You've gone off your food.
  • You haven't opened your bowels today. You normally go once a day.

Say no to all of these if asked:

  • Diarrhoea, a swollen or bloated tummy.
  • Blood in your poo, or black tarry poo.
  • Weight loss or tiredness.
  • Pain going through to your back, heartburn, pain under the right ribs, or pain after fatty food.
  • Taking anti-inflammatories (Nurofen, Voltaren).
  • Pain going from your loin to your groin, blood in your urine, burning when passing urine, or passing urine more often.
  • Sweats, chills or shaking (rigors).

Context (only if asked): no recent travel, nobody around you has been sick, and no food you think was off. You've never had a bowel problem and never had tummy surgery. You've never had gallstones. If asked whether you drink heavily: "No, not really."

Past medical history: asthma. No operations.

Medications: salbutamol (Ventolin) puffer when needed. Nothing else.

Allergies: penicillin: you got an itchy rash as a child a few days into a course of amoxicillin; no swelling or breathing trouble.

Family history: your mum has Crohn's disease.

Social history:

  • You live with your parents.
  • You work full time as a teacher.
  • You are vegan and walk the dog every day.
  • Alcohol, only if asked how much: 3 beers a day.
  • You don't smoke and don't take any drugs.
  • If asked: you are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.
  • If asked how you got here or who could take you: you drove yourself; your mum is at home and could come and get you.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: "Mum has Crohn's. Is this my bowel?"
  • Concern: you are worried you will need your colon (bowel) removed.
  • Expectation: you want to know what's going on and want something for the pain.

Question to raise once in Part 1: "Is this Crohn's, like Mum?"

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: looks unwell and flushed, lying still, winces when he shifts or coughs. Alert. Weight 78 kg.
  • Observations (10:20): temperature 37.9 °C, HR 102 regular, BP 128/78, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, capillary BGL 5.6 mmol/L, pain 7/10.
  • Hydration: mucous membranes slightly dry, CRT 2 seconds.
  • Hands, eyes, mouth: no clubbing, pallor or jaundice. No mouth ulcers.
  • Chest and heart: chest clear, no wheeze. Heart sounds dual, no murmurs.
  • Abdomen, inspection: not distended, no scars. He breathes shallowly to avoid moving his abdomen.
  • Abdomen, palpation: tender around the umbilicus and in the right iliac fossa, maximal at McBurney's point, with voluntary guarding in the right iliac fossa. No rigidity. No masses, no hepatosplenomegaly. Murphy's sign negative. Left iliac fossa non-tender.
  • Peritonism: percussion tenderness and rebound tenderness in the right iliac fossa. Pain in the right iliac fossa when he coughs.
  • Special signs: Rovsing's sign positive (pressing the left iliac fossa causes right iliac fossa pain). Psoas and obturator signs negative.
  • Bowel sounds: present, slightly reduced.
  • Renal angles: non-tender.
  • Hernial orifices: clear.
  • Genitals (if offered with a chaperone): testes normal lie, non-tender, no swelling.
  • Rectal examination (if offered with a chaperone): tenderness on the right side, brown stool, no blood.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Daniel's identity, gains consent, and asks whether he is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin.
Acknowledges his pain early (offers analgesia or a comfortable position), uses plain language and responds with empathy to his worry about his bowel.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: lower abdomen, worst around the umbilicus, no radiation.
Onset and time course: started 12 hours ago, gradual, constant and unchanged, never had it before.
Character and severity: dull and vague, 7/10, has hardly done anything since.
Aggravating and relieving factors: worse with coughing and movement, nothing relieves it.

check.x: Asks about associated gastrointestinal and systemic symptoms:

kids.x: Nausea, vomiting (vomited breakfast) and loss of appetite.
Fever (felt, not measured), and sweats, chills or rigors (none).
Bowel habit: no bowel motion today (usually once a day), no diarrhoea, no blood or melaena, no distension.

check.x: Asks at least two context questions: travel, sick contacts or suspect food (none), previous bowel conditions or abdominal surgery (none).
check.d: Award for at least two context questions.

check.x: Screens at least three other systems for alternative causes: pancreatic, biliary and upper GI (back radiation, heartburn, melaena, fatty-food or right upper quadrant pain, gallstones); renal tract (loin-to-groin pain, haematuria, dysuria, frequency); inflammatory bowel disease (weight loss, fatigue, blood in the stool).
check.d: Award for features asked from at least three systems.

check.x: Takes the past medical and medication history: asthma, no surgery, salbutamol as needed, no NSAIDs.
Asks about allergies and clarifies the reaction: penicillin, an itchy rash a few days into amoxicillin as a child, with no swelling or breathing trouble.
Takes a family history: his mother has Crohn's disease.
Takes a social history: lives with his parents, full-time teacher, vegan, walks the dog daily, no smoking or drugs, and quantifies alcohol (3 beers a day) rather than accepting 'not heavily'.
check.d: Award for living situation or occupation, smoking/drugs, and alcohol quantified (3 beers a day); diet and exercise not required.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: wonders whether it is Crohn's like his mother, worried his colon will be removed, wants answers and pain relief.
Examination
Asks for a full set of vital signs and identifies the raised temperature (37.9 °C, borderline/low-grade) and tachycardia (HR 102).
Inspects generally and assesses hydration: lying still, pain on moving, mildly dry mucous membranes, CRT 2 seconds.
Examines the abdomen:

kids.x: Inspects, and palpates all regions starting away from the pain.
Finds tenderness maximal at McBurney's point in the right iliac fossa with guarding.
Tests gently for peritonism (percussion or rebound tenderness, or pain on coughing).
kids.d: Credit percussion tenderness as the gentler test.

kids.x: Tests Rovsing's, psoas or obturator signs, and listens for bowel sounds.
kids.d: Award for at least one special sign plus bowel sounds.

check.x: Checks for other causes: Murphy's sign, renal angles, hernial orifices, and offers a testicular examination with a chaperone.
Summarises the examination: raised temperature and tachycardia with localised right iliac fossa tenderness and peritonism.
Interpretation

Interprets the repeat observations: temperature up from 37.9 to 38.2 °C, HR up from 102 to 110, pain 8/10 and further vomiting over about 35 minutes. He is getting worse, so he needs hospital now, not watchful waiting at home.

Interprets the urine dipstick: no blood, leucocytes or nitrites (against renal colic and urinary tract infection); ketones and a high-normal specific gravity fit vomiting and poor intake. States that a normal dipstick does not rule appendicitis in or out.

Gives acute appendicitis as the most likely diagnosis and justifies it: constant dull periumbilical pain with nausea, vomiting, anorexia and fever, pain on coughing and movement, and right iliac fossa tenderness with peritonism.
Gives differentials, each with a feature for or against:
check.d: Also credit other reasonable differentials (e.g. testicular torsion, Meckel's diverticulitis, mesenteric adenitis) given with a feature for or against, up to the same marks.

kids.x: Acute pancreatitis: nausea, vomiting, fever and 3 beers a day; against: the site and character don't fit (no epigastric pain or back radiation).
Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's): mother has Crohn's and he has systemic symptoms; against: no weight loss or blood, and the course is too short.
Less likely: gastroenteritis (no diarrhoea or contacts), bowel obstruction (no distension) and renal colic (no loin-to-groin pain, urinary symptoms or blood on dipstick).
kids.d: Award for at least two of the three with a feature against.

check.x: Management

Recognises a likely surgical emergency, informs the supervising GP and refers him to the ED the same day, now: phones the ED or on-call surgical registrar with an ISBAR handover and sends a referral letter that includes the penicillin allergy.
Keeps him nil by mouth in case he needs theatre.
Offers analgesia and an antiemetic before transfer, and explains that pain relief does not hide the diagnosis.
check.d: Accept any reasonable analgesic and antiemetic available in the practice, e.g. paracetamol 1 g oral with a sip of water, methoxyflurane, or IM morphine per practice protocol; ondansetron 4 mg wafer or IM/IV, or metoclopramide 10 mg IM/IV. Small sips to take medicines are acceptable while nil by mouth. Credit caution with NSAIDs in a patient with asthma.

check.x: Arranges safe transport: an ambulance given the rising heart rate and fever, or a parent driving him straight to the ED if the supervising GP judges him stable. He must not drive himself.
check.d: Accept either option with a reason; the item is lost if he is allowed to drive.

check.x: Briefly tells Daniel what to expect in hospital: bloods, imaging if the diagnosis is uncertain, IV fluids, surgical review with antibiotics, and usually laparoscopic appendicectomy.
check.d: Award for any three of: bloods, imaging if the diagnosis is uncertain, IV fluids, surgical review with antibiotics, laparoscopic appendicectomy.

check.x: Answers his worry in plain words: the appendix is a small pouch off the start of the large bowel, and removing it is keyhole surgery that does not remove the colon; this picture doesn't fit Crohn's, but the team will look for it.
check.d: Credit the Crohn's explanation whether given in Part 1, when Daniel asks, or in Part 2.

check.x: Explains the cause in plain words: the inside of the appendix becomes blocked (for example by a hard, sometimes calcified lump of faeces, a faecolith, or swollen lymph tissue), so it swells and becomes infected.
check.d: Accept any plain explanation of blockage leading to swelling and infection.

check.x: Explains the complications:

kids.x: Names at least two: perforation, peritonitis, appendiceal abscess, appendiceal mass, surgical site infection.
Explains them clearly in plain words (for example the appendix can burst and spread infection through the abdomen).

check.x: Safety netting

Tells him to call 000 if, before or on the way to hospital, the pain suddenly gets much worse or spreads across his whole tummy, his tummy goes hard, he can't stop vomiting, he gets shakes or rigors, or he feels faint or confused.
check.d: Award for at least three red flags in plain words, linked to calling 000.

check.x: Tells him when and where to come back if he is sent home from ED without surgery: return to ED if the pain worsens or spreads, the fever or vomiting gets worse, or he cannot keep fluids down.
Arranges follow-up: asks him to see the GP after discharge to review his recovery (and wound, if operated on), and to discuss his alcohol intake (3 beers a day is above the NHMRC guideline).
check.d: Award for a GP review after discharge; the alcohol discussion is a bonus, not required.

part2.lead: While you were taking the history, the practice nurse tested Daniel's urine. She has just repeated his observations. Here they are.
part2.patient:
Ask this once, while the candidate explains the plan:

  • "Are they going to have to take out my bowel?"

You are relieved if told it is the appendix and not the colon. If the candidate uses jargon such as "appendicectomy", "peritonitis" or "faecolith" without explaining it, ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Room air throughout. First set taken at the start of the consultation; repeat set taken by the practice nurse about 35 minutes later. No medicines given yet (analgesia awaiting GP review).
handover.model:
• Read: general practice has no zoned observation chart, so read the trend. Temperature has risen from 37.9 to 38.2 °C (fever) and HR from 102 to 110 (tachycardia). RR has gone from 18 to 20, pain from 7 to 8/10, and he has vomited again. BP 124/76 and SpO2 98% are normal, and he is alert.
  • For Daniel: a systemic inflammatory response that is getting worse over half an hour, which fits progressing appendicitis. He is not shocked.
  • What it changes: he needs the ED now, with nothing by mouth. The rising HR and fever support sending him by ambulance. A falling BP, HR still climbing, rigors or confusion mean a 000 call and suspected sepsis or perforation.

rows.note: Repeat set; vomited once in the treatment room

handover.label: Urine dipstick
handover.result: Midstream urine, dipstick tested at the practice at 10:40.
handover.model:
• Read: no blood, leucocytes or nitrites. Protein, glucose and bilirubin are negative. Ketones 1+, specific gravity 1.025.
  • For Daniel: no haematuria, which argues against a ureteric stone. No leucocytes or nitrites, which argues against urinary tract infection. Ketones and concentrated urine fit vomiting and not eating. Glucose negative.
  • What it changes: it does not rule appendicitis in or out. An inflamed appendix lying next to the ureter or bladder can cause a few white or red cells in the urine, so an abnormal dipstick would not have excluded it either. Formal urine microscopy can be done at the hospital. He needs IV fluids in hospital, because he is to stay nil by mouth.

ask: You are now calling the on-call general surgical registrar at the local hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Daniel Lando, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Daniel now, here in general practice.
Daniel asks you what has caused this and what complications it could lead to. Please answer him, then tell me what you would advise him before he leaves the practice.
expect:
• Identify: self (medical student with the GP), practice; Daniel Lando, 32.
  • Situation: probable acute appendicitis; referring him to ED now for surgical review.
  • Background: 12 hours of constant dull periumbilical pain, 7/10, worse with coughing and movement; nausea, vomiting, anorexia, fever. Asthma on salbutamol. Penicillin allergy (delayed itchy rash in childhood, no swelling or breathing trouble). 3 beers a day.
  • Assessment: right iliac fossa tenderness at McBurney's point with guarding, rebound and positive Rovsing's. Temperature up from 37.9 to 38.2 °C, HR up from 102 to 110, BP and SpO2 normal: worsening, not shocked. Urine dipstick: no blood or leucocytes, ketones 1+.
  • Recommendation: please accept him for review in ED; he is nil by mouth and will come by ambulance (or with a parent if the GP judges him stable); bloods, IV fluids and assessment for theatre.

Most likely: acute appendicitis. Constant dull periumbilical pain for 12 hours with nausea, vomiting, anorexia and fever; pain on coughing and movement; right iliac fossa tenderness with peritonism and positive Rovsing's; rising temperature and HR. He hasn't noticed the pain move to the right iliac fossa yet, but the examination shows it is localising.

  • Acute pancreatitis: for: vomiting, fever, 3 beers a day. Against: the site and character don't fit, and no back radiation.
  • Crohn's disease: for: mother has Crohn's, systemic symptoms. Against: no weight loss or blood, and too short a history.
  • Less likely: gastroenteritis (no diarrhoea or contacts), bowel obstruction (no distension), renal colic (no loin-to-groin pain or haematuria).

1. Same-day, urgent referral to ED: phone the ED or surgical registrar, involve the supervising GP, and send a referral letter including the penicillin allergy.
  2. Nil by mouth.
  3. Analgesia and an antiemetic before transfer; pain relief does not mask the diagnosis.
  4. Transport: ambulance (rising HR and fever), or a parent drives him straight to ED if stable. He does not drive himself.
  5. Explain to Daniel: the appendix, not the colon. Keyhole appendicectomy is usual. This picture doesn't fit Crohn's, but the hospital team will consider it. In hospital: bloods (FBC, CRP, UEC, LFTs, lipase), imaging if the diagnosis is uncertain, IV fluids and antibiotics.

• Cause: the inside of the appendix gets blocked, for example by a faecolith (a small, hard, sometimes calcified lump of poo) or swollen lymph tissue, so it swells and becomes infected.
  • Complications (at least two, in plain words): it can burst (perforation) and spread infection through the abdomen (peritonitis), or form an abscess or an inflamed mass. After surgery, the wound can become infected.
  • Call 000 if the pain suddenly gets much worse or spreads across the whole abdomen, the abdomen goes hard, he keeps vomiting, has rigors, or feels faint or confused.
  • If sent home from ED without surgery, return to ED if the pain worsens or spreads, the fever or vomiting gets worse, or he cannot keep fluids down.
  • Follow-up: see the GP after discharge to review his recovery (and wound, if operated on), and to talk about his alcohol intake.

ddx.for: Constant dull periumbilical pain for 12 hours with nausea, vomiting, anorexia and fever, pain on coughing and movement, and right iliac fossa tenderness with rebound and a positive Rovsing's sign.
ddx.against: He hasn't noticed the pain moving to the right iliac fossa yet.

ddx.for: Nausea, vomiting and fever in a man who drinks 3 beers a day.
ddx.against: Lower abdominal and periumbilical rather than epigastric pain, no back radiation, and no gallstones.

ddx.for: His mother has Crohn's disease, and he has right iliac fossa pain with fever.
ddx.against: No weight loss, fatigue, diarrhoea or blood in the stool, and only a 12-hour history.
No diarrhoea, no sick contacts, travel or suspect food, and localised peritonism.

ddx.for: Vomiting and no bowel motion today.
ddx.against: No distension, bowel sounds present, and no previous abdominal surgery.

ddx.for: Acute lower abdominal pain with vomiting.
ddx.against: Constant dull pain without loin-to-groin radiation, no urinary symptoms, non-tender renal angles and no blood on the dipstick.

guide:
This is a general practice station, so there is no observation chart. Give the first set of observations from the Exam findings when the candidate asks for them. In Part 1, the examiner gives findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. If the candidate asks for tests in Part 1, say the urine is being tested by the nurse and the results will come in Part 2. Bloods and imaging would be done in hospital. The nurse repeats the observations whatever the candidate does. If the candidate offers analgesia in Part 1, say the supervising GP will prescribe it once the assessment is complete; the repeat observations are taken before any is given. In Part 2, hand over both results, then ask the four questions in order. Daniel asks his question about his bowel once, while the candidate explains the plan.

Credit the source's differentials (pancreatitis, IBD, gastroenteritis, obstruction, renal colic) when they come with a feature for or against.

A high-performing candidate characterises the pain fully and picks up the pain on coughing and movement. They cover nausea, vomiting, anorexia and fever, screen several systems, quantify his alcohol and clarify his penicillin allergy. They examine the abdomen gently, find the McBurney's point tenderness and peritonism, and check the hernial orifices and testes. In Part 2 they see that he is getting worse, call it appendicitis, and send him to ED now with nil by mouth, analgesia and safe transport. They reassure him that his colon will not be removed, explain the cause and the complications in plain words, give clear 000 red flags, and arrange GP follow-up.

A borderline candidate takes a generic history, misses the fever or peritonism, or calls it gastroenteritis or Crohn's and plans outpatient tests or "review tomorrow". They may withhold analgesia, let him eat, let him drive himself, or use jargon without explaining it.
explain:
Diagnosis

Daniel most likely has acute appendicitis. Twelve hours of constant, dull, poorly localised periumbilical pain with nausea, vomiting, anorexia and fever is the classic early picture. The pain is worse with coughing and movement, which suggests the peritoneum is inflamed. On examination there is tenderness at McBurney's point with guarding, rebound and a positive Rovsing's sign, and his temperature and heart rate rise while he is in the practice.

Why the pain moves

Early on, the swollen appendix stretches its own wall. Visceral afferent nerves (midgut, around T10) carry this as vague periumbilical pain. As inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum, which has somatic nerves, the pain localises to the right iliac fossa. This is the classic migratory pain. Daniel hasn't felt the pain move yet, but his examination already shows localised peritonism. That is why examining the abdomen matters even when the history sounds vague.

Cause

Appendicitis follows obstruction of the appendix lumen, often by a faecolith (a hardened, sometimes calcified lump of faeces). Lymphoid hyperplasia is another cause in young people, and often no obstructing cause is found. The blocked lumen fills with mucus, bacteria overgrow, pressure rises, and the wall becomes inflamed, ischaemic and eventually gangrenous or perforated.

Complications

  • Perforation: more likely the longer the diagnosis is delayed.
  • Peritonitis: localised or generalised, with a risk of sepsis.
  • Appendiceal abscess or an appendiceal mass (an inflammatory phlegmon wrapped in omentum and bowel).
  • Surgical site infection after appendicectomy.

Differentials that matter

  • Acute pancreatitis: his regular drinking, vomiting and fever fit, but the pain is in the wrong place and has the wrong character. A normal lipase in ED makes it very unlikely.
  • Inflammatory bowel disease: ileocaecal Crohn's disease can mimic appendicitis, and his mother has Crohn's. However, he has no weight loss, diarrhoea or blood, and a 12-hour history is too short.
  • Less likely: gastroenteritis (no diarrhoea or contacts), bowel obstruction (no distension or previous surgery) and ureteric colic (no loin-to-groin pain or haematuria). In a young man, the hernial orifices and testes are examined so that a strangulated hernia or testicular torsion is not missed.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: the rising temperature and heart rate over 35 minutes show a worsening inflammatory response. Blood pressure and oxygen saturation are normal, so he is not shocked, but he should not be sent home to wait.
  • Urine dipstick: no blood, leucocytes or nitrites, so a stone or urinary infection is less likely. Ketones reflect vomiting and fasting. An inflamed appendix next to the ureter or bladder can cause some pyuria or haematuria, so the dipstick neither confirms nor excludes appendicitis.

Management in general practice

Suspected appendicitis is a surgical emergency, and the GP's job is to get him to hospital safely. Refer him the same day to the ED or the surgical team with a phone handover and a letter that includes his penicillin allergy. Keep him nil by mouth. Offer analgesia and an antiemetic: adequate analgesia does not hide the signs of an acute abdomen. Arrange safe transport. An ambulance is reasonable given his rising heart rate and fever, and he must not drive himself.

What happens in hospital

In hospital he will have bloods (FBC, CRP, electrolytes, liver tests, lipase), IV fluids, analgesia and a surgical review. Imaging (ultrasound or CT) is used when the diagnosis is uncertain. Clinical scores such as the Alvarado or the Appendicitis Inflammatory Response score combine symptoms, signs and blood results to stratify risk. Treatment is usually laparoscopic appendicectomy with antibiotics given before surgery (eTG). His penicillin allergy (a delayed itchy rash in childhood, with no swelling or breathing trouble) is taken into account when antibiotics are chosen, which is why the type of reaction matters. This is a low-risk, non-severe delayed reaction, so per eTG cefazolin (with metronidazole) can usually still be used, and he may be suitable for later penicillin allergy delabelling. Antibiotics alone are an option for selected patients with uncomplicated appendicitis, decided by the surgical team (WSES). The colon is not removed. People live normally without an appendix.

Safety netting and follow-up

He should call 000 if the pain suddenly worsens or spreads across his whole abdomen, the abdomen becomes rigid, the vomiting is uncontrolled, he has rigors, or he feels faint or confused. These suggest perforation or sepsis. If he is sent home without surgery, he should return if the pain worsens or spreads, the fever or vomiting gets worse, or he cannot keep fluids down. At GP follow-up after discharge, it is worth raising his alcohol intake: 3 beers a day is above the NHMRC guideline of no more than 10 standard drinks a week.
points: Early appendicitis causes vague, constant periumbilical pain (visceral afferents) that later localises to the right iliac fossa as the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed.
Anorexia, nausea and vomiting, fever, pain on coughing or movement, and McBurney's point tenderness with peritonism make appendicitis likely even before the patient notices the pain move.

Appendicitis follows obstruction of the appendix lumen (for example by a faecolith or lymphoid hyperplasia); complications include perforation, peritonitis, abscess, appendiceal mass and surgical site infection.
In general practice, suspected appendicitis needs same-day referral to ED: phone handover, nil by mouth, analgesia (which does not mask the diagnosis), safe transport and documented allergies.
A normal urine dipstick does not exclude appendicitis, and an inflamed appendix near the ureter or bladder can cause mild pyuria or haematuria.
Rising temperature and heart rate during a consultation mean the patient is getting worse and should not be sent home to wait.
